proposal: The Mandate recommends amending the Higher Education Act to bar accreditors from using their Title IV gatekeeper role to require diversity policies or to intrude on state or religious institution governance, and to let states recognize accreditors. It also recommends that the Secretary decline to recognize accreditors that abuse their power, encourage new accreditors, and that the President pursue antitrust action against accreditors, especially the American Bar Association.

source_checks.note: Executive Order 14279 (2025-04-23) directs the Secretary to hold accreditors accountable through recognition actions, address accreditor-required discrimination, keep accreditors from pushing violations of state law, streamline switching and resume recognizing new accreditors, and to assess whether to suspend or terminate the ABA council's recognition; it directs the Attorney General to investigate discrimination by law and medical schools and does not mention antitrust.

Proposed rule published 2026-08-20 (comments closed 2026-09-21, 7,051 received) that reflects negotiated rulemaking consensus of 2026-05-21 and implements Executive Order 14279: removes geographic limits, bars standards that direct institutions to break federal or state law, requires viewpoint neutrality except for religious-mission agencies and eases switching. It replaces rather than simply drops the two-year rule, does not mention the ABA, and proposes a section stating that recognition gives no antitrust immunity, which the record omitted.

significance.rationale: Reforming accreditation and opening the field to new accreditors changes the gatekeeping rules for colleges.

status_summary: As of 2026-10-07 the executive and rulemaking track is under way, while the Mandate's statutory changes are not. Executive Order 14279 (2025-04-23) directed ED to hold accreditors accountable under the recognition criteria, ensure they do not require discrimination barred by law, speed institutions' switching of accreditors, resume recognizing new accreditors, and assess the American Bar Association council's recognition. ED published a nonbinding interpretive rule on initial recognition of new accreditors on 2026-02-27. After a negotiated rulemaking committee reached consensus on 2026-05-21, ED proposed regulations on 2026-08-20 that would remove geographic limits on accreditors, replace the two-year rule for initial recognition with a check that ends recognition if no institution relies on the agency two years after recognition, bar standards that direct institutions to violate federal or state law, require viewpoint neutrality except for agencies with a religious mission, and state that federal recognition gives accreditors no immunity from antitrust laws; comments closed 2026-09-21 with 7,051 received and no final rule has been published. Six public university systems have formed a new accreditor, the Commission for Public Higher Education, which per a trade report has not applied for federal recognition and plans to file in late 2027. ED's advisory committee scheduled renewal reviews of the ABA council and SACSCOC for 2026-09-23 and 2026-09-24; the outcome was not found.

timeline.event: Executive Order 14279 directs the Education Secretary to enforce recognition criteria against accreditors, ensure accreditors do not require discrimination barred by law or push violations of state law, streamline switching of accreditors, resume recognizing new accreditors, and assess whether to suspend or end recognition of the ABA's law school accreditation council; it directs the Attorney General to investigate alleged discrimination by ABA-linked law schools.

ED publishes a nonbinding interpretive rule on initial recognition of accreditors, stating its reading of the criteria and review timing for new agencies and citing Executive Order 14279; the rule keeps a two-year period that starts at a new agency's first accrediting activity.

Higher Ed Dive reports that the Commission for Public Higher Education, founded by six public university systems (Florida, Texas A&M, North Carolina, South Carolina, Tennessee, Georgia), has not applied for federal recognition and plans to file in late 2027, and that a federal grant of 1 million dollars lets it waive dues until recognition.

ED publishes the proposed rule 'Accreditation, Innovation, and Modernization' amending 34 CFR parts 600, 602 and 668. It reflects the consensus of the negotiated rulemaking committee (announced 2026-01-27; sessions in April and May 2026; consensus 2026-05-21) and proposes removing geographic limits on accreditors, dropping the two-year rule for initial recognition, barring standards that push institutions to violate federal or state law, requiring viewpoint-neutral decisions except for agencies with a religious mission, and easing institutions' switching of accreditors. Comments closed 2026-09-21 with 7,051 received.

ED notices a 2026-09-23 and 2026-09-24 meeting of its accreditation advisory committee (NACIQI) to review renewal of recognition for six agencies, including the ABA's law school accreditation council and the Southern Association's Commission on Colleges, plus one compliance report.

title: Reform accreditation: curb non-academic mandates and open the field to new accreditors
uncertainties: The proposed rule was read through its first 100,000 characters only (the rest, about 40,000 characters, was not read), so some provisions may be missing from the summary; the page text did not mention the ABA or the word DEI. The January 2026 negotiated rulemaking announcement is cited through the proposed rule, not read directly. Outcomes of the 2026-09-23 and 2026-09-24 advisory committee review were not found. No search found a derecognition, suspension or antitrust action against an accreditor, but no search was run for these specifically beyond one web search on new accreditors and the ABA council.
